question: What is the primary medical term for infective bone disease?
explanation: Osteomyelitis specifically denotes inflammation and infection of the bone and bone marrow caused by infectious agents. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h1)

question: Why does infection within the bone cortex rapidly lead to tissue death?

options.A: Calcium deposits instantly precipitate and block nerve pathways
options.B: Bone marrow tissue has no white blood cells to fight pathogens
options.C: Bacterial toxins directly dissolve all surrounding muscle fibers
options.D: Increased intraosseous pressure causes microvascular thrombosis and ischemia

explanation: The rigid, non-expanding nature of bone walls means inflammation causes pressure to rise quickly, compressing local blood vessels and cutting off nutrient supplies. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h1)

question: What term describes a segment of necrotic bone that has become separated from living bone tissue?
explanation: A sequestrum is dead bone resulting from ischemia caused by periosteal stripping and vascular thrombosis during infection. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h2)

question: What is the physiological origin of an involucrum in chronic osteomyelitis?

options.A: Accumulated bacterial colonies calcifying within the medullary cavity
options.B: New bone formation laid down by the living periosteum around the infected site
options.C: Deposition of fibrous cartilage replacing destroyed muscle attachments
options.D: Scars formed by overlying skin that has healed over a chronic sinus tract

explanation: The periosteum responds to subperiosteal pus accumulation by generating a sleeve of new bone designed to wall off the infection. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h2)

question: Which microorganism is the most frequent causative agent of osteomyelitis across all age groups?
explanation: Staphylococcus aureus possesses specific surface adhesion molecules that allow it to bind to bone matrix proteins, making it the predominant pathogen in bone infections. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h3)

question: A patient with sickle cell disease presents with osteomyelitis. Which specific bacterium should clinicians strongly suspect alongside Staphylococcus aureus?
explanation: Individuals with sickle cell disease have functional asplenia and micro-infarctions in the gut and bone, predisposing them uniquely to Salmonella osteomyelitis. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h3)

question: What is a hallmark local symptom reported by a patient with acute osteomyelitis?

options.A: Complete paralysis of the affected limb within hours
options.B: Intermittent numbness confined strictly to the fingertips
options.C: Painless, rapid swelling without any skin discoloration
options.D: Constant, throbbing bone pain aggravated by movement

explanation: Rising pressure within the rigid bone cortex causes a characteristic deep, constant, throbbing pain that worsens with physical activity. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h4)

question: Which finding is most characteristic of chronic osteomyelitis compared to acute presentation?

options.A: Complete absence of pain due to nerve destruction
options.B: Immediate joint laxity and total ligament rupture
options.C: Presence of draining sinus tracts discharging pus
options.D: Sudden onset of high spiking fevers and severe rigors

explanation: Chronic cases often feature persistent sinus tracts that intermittently discharge purulent material from deep necrotic bone foci. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h4)

question: Why are plain radiographs of limited use in diagnosing acute osteomyelitis during the first week of symptoms?

options.A: X-ray machines cannot penetrate deep bone tissue in adult limbs
options.B: Calcium deposits temporarily disappear from view during acute inflammation
options.C: Radiation exposure instantly destroys any bacteria present in the marrow
options.D: Significant bone destruction must occur before it becomes visible on X-ray

explanation: At least thirty to fifty percent of bone matrix must be lost before radiographic changes like lucency or periosteal reaction become visible, taking up to two weeks. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h5)

question: Which diagnostic procedure is considered the definitive standard for identifying the exact causative organism in osteomyelitis?

options.B: Ultrasound of the affected muscle bellies

explanation: Obtaining a direct sample of the infected bone via biopsy ensures targeted antibiotic therapy based on definitive organism isolation and sensitivity testing. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h5)

question: What is the typical duration of antibiotic therapy required to effectively treat osteomyelitis?

options.B: Four to six weeks or longer

explanation: Because bone has poor vascular penetration compared to other tissues, prolonged antibiotic courses are necessary to clear deep-seated infection. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h6)

question: When should broad-spectrum empiric antibiotics be started in a patient with suspected acute osteomyelitis?

options.A: Immediately after blood and bone cultures are collected
options.B: After all imaging modalities have been completed and reviewed
options.C: Only after final laboratory sensitivity reports return in two weeks
options.D: When the patient develops chronic sinus tract formation

explanation: Cultures must be drawn first to avoid skewing results, but treatment should start promptly to prevent rapid bone necrosis and systemic sepsis. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h6)

question: What is the primary goal of surgical debridement in the management of chronic osteomyelitis?

options.A: Removal of all devitalized, infected bone and necrotic tissue
options.B: Permanent fusion of the nearest healthy joint to prevent movement
options.C: Complete removal of the periosteum from the entire long bone
options.D: Replacement of bone marrow with synthetic liquid polymers

explanation: Debridement eliminates the avascular sequestrum where bacteria hide and survive away from systemic antibiotics and host immune cells. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h7)

question: What is the therapeutic purpose of placing antibiotic-impregnated cement beads into a bone defect during surgery?

options.A: To permanently replace the structural strength of the missing bone cortex
options.B: To prevent the skin from adhering to deep muscle layers
options.C: To deliver high local concentrations of medication directly to the infection site
options.D: To stimulate rapid cartilage growth across the joint space

explanation: Cement beads release antibiotics locally into the avascular dead space where systemic blood supply cannot deliver adequate drug concentrations. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h7)

question: Which dietary component should nurses emphasize when educating a patient recovering from bone infection and surgery?

options.A: Elimination of all dairy and calcium sources
options.B: High protein and vitamins to support tissue healing
options.C: Strictly restricted fluid intake to prevent edema
options.D: Low calorie intake to reduce body weight on the limb

explanation: Tissue repair, collagen synthesis, and bone matrix regeneration demand increased metabolic and nutritional support, particularly high protein and vitamin intake. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h8)

question: What critical instruction must be given to a patient discharged home on a multi-week course of oral antibiotics?

options.A: Double the dose if a single daily pill is accidentally missed
options.B: Complete the entire prescribed course even if symptoms disappear early
options.C: Switch to over-the-counter herbal alternatives after two weeks
options.D: Stop taking the medication as soon as pain subsides to save doses

explanation: Premature cessation of antibiotics allows resilient bacterial survivors to multiply, leading directly to recurrent or chronic treatment-resistant osteomyelitis. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h8)

question: What is a major structural complication associated with extensive chronic bone infection?
explanation: Extensive bone destruction and necrosis compromise structural integrity, predisposing the weakened bone to fracture under normal weight-bearing forces. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h9)

question: Which malignant transformation is a recognized long-term risk associated with chronic, unhealed draining sinus tracts?
explanation: Chronic irritation and inflammation from long-standing sinus tracts or burn scars can precipitate squamous cell carcinoma, termed a Marjolin ulcer. [learn more](GNS222_U1_T17#GNS222_U1_T17_h9)
